reason: Small heads are a normal description of a capitulum.
Capillary means thin and thread-like. Fibrillary is the nearest PATO shape, and it fits stolons and rhizoids in bryophytes and ferns. I did not check the PATO definition.
A branch or twig can taper.
The style, or its apex, can be rugose or rugulose. Some examples are bare French adjectives such as 'rugueuses', so the bearer there is not certain.

The examples mix arrangement within the inflorescence (axillary, terminal, widely spaced), orientation (erect to patent) and 'secund'. A rule would have to send each of these to its own attribute: arrangement, orientation or position. Plain 'position' is too generic.
Wrong reading. 'Margin ciliate-dentate' describes the margin of a leaf or other organ, and a trichome has no teeth. The bearer 'shoot axis trichome' comes from 'ciliate'.

Wrong reading. 'Inflorescence a compound anthela' names the type of the inflorescence and does not say an anthela is present. Handle it with the inflorescence-type pattern, not as a presence quality of the anthela.
Gemmae have measured length. The examples are length × width.
Sori can be continuous, for example running along the segment margin.
Spores can be spiny or echinate, and the perispore is part of the spore.
Involucral bracts, or phyllaries, can be leaf-like (foliaceous).
An ovary can be spiny or echinate. Some examples describe echinate hairs, which should be a bristly or hairy quality instead.
An awn can be deciduous or caducous.
A style can be plumose, as in many Asteraceae and grasses.
The corolla lip can be hairy. Pilosity is the attribute and the examples give its values.
A floral disc can be inconspicuous or obscure.
A receptacle can be fimbriate or have a fimbriate appendage. The appendage cases need the has-part reading.
Peristome teeth are split into divisions or prongs.
Bud scales can be inconspicuous. Only one flora supports this pair.
Wrong reading. The counted items are rows of cells, not limbidia, so the amount belongs to the cell rows. Use the counted-part rule for 'rows of cells' instead.
Wrong reading. A spurred costa has spurs as parts and is not shaped like a spur. Spurred should become has-part spur, and only a shape such as 'spur shaped' should use this PATO term.

Wrong reading. The examples are mostly 'angled', which means ridged or angular in section, and it was mapped to 'bent'. A petiole truly bent near the apex is rare, and a rule would have to separate those cases.
A lamina can be bifid or bifurcate at the apex. The examples show a bifid apex, which is a looser sense of 'forked'.
Wrong reading. Anther spurs are parts of the anther, and the anther itself is not spur shaped. Use has-part spur.
A connective can be prolonged or longer than the pollen sacs.
Wrong attribute. A seta is measured as length (PATO_0000122), and the examples '1–3 cm' are lengths. Height fits an erect plant, not a seta.
The abaxial surface of a sepal can be hairy.
Sepals can be ligulate or strap-shaped.
A style can be entire, meaning undivided. The PATO term's definition should be checked, because 'entire' often means a margin. Some examples ('entire length') are not about the style.
A flower bract has a width, given with its length.
Phyllaries can be persistent.
An awn can be toothed. In 'toothed awn' the awn is the bearer and the teeth are its quality.
A pinnule apex can be acuminate.
A petal apex can be retuse.
An ovary can be bristly.
An anther can be narrow. A few examples are about the connective, which is a different bearer.
A lateral vein can fork (furcate).
A branch or twig can be setose.
An orchid labellum or its apex can be entire.
A style can be small or minute.
A leaf lobe can be pubescent.

The generic 'texture' is paired with different readings: sulcate is a shape (groove), and papillose is a surface texture. A rule would need the specific term to choose the right attribute, so texture alone should not be allowed.
A pappus can be coroniform, or crown-like.
An achene apex or base can be obtuse. Some examples are 'rounded' and may belong to the keel.
A pedicel can be flexuous or sinuous.
Lenticels can be inconspicuous or obscure.
The adaxial side of a petal can have its own colour.
A lobe base can be cuneate.
A leaf sheath can split.
Phyllaries can be spiny or unarmed. The negated examples need the negation rule.
A thorn can be reflexed. Some examples are about spines on other parts, such as the leaf.
A corolla lip can be grooved or canaliculate.
A peduncle can be spreading.
The number of berries per infructescence is an amount of berries.
A frond can be glabrous.
A tuber can be subglobose or spheroid.
A floral disc can be thin.
Rhizoids can be capillary (thread-like). This follows the stolon pair, so decide both together.
An operculum has a width, given with its length.
Fronds can be arching.
